thread.think.behind: Where does thinking come from: the parts, or how they are arranged?
thread.strange.root: What is the strangest thing that could compute?
thread.strange.behind: Is computing something we invented, or something nature was already doing?
thread.limit.root: What could a chip never do, and could it learn to?
thread.limit.behind: Can a creation go beyond its creator?
thread.fail.root: Why can a perfect design fail in the real world?
thread.fail.behind: Is "perfect" only possible inside our models?
thread.idea.root: How could your idea become a chip?
thread.idea.behind: How do ideas become real, and who gets to make them?
thread.make.root: What would chipmaking look like if we invented it from scratch today?
thread.make.behind: How much of our technology is the way it is only because of history?
thread.know.root: What part of making chips can't be written down?
thread.know.behind: How much expertise lives only in people's hands, and can AI ever capture it?
thread.open.root: What happens when anyone can make a chip?
thread.open.behind: What happens to a society when powerful tools reach everyone?
thread.divide.root: How should a chip divide its work?
thread.divide.behind: How should any system divide work: cells, companies, societies?
thread.life.root: What new kinds of computers could brains, swarms and living cells inspire?
thread.life.behind: If we stopped copying the 80-year-old computer design, what would we copy instead?
thread.scale.root: What will be the next Moore's law?
thread.scale.behind: Can any kind of progress keep doubling forever?
stop.think.rack.q: An AI answers you from a rack like this. Where in here is the thinking?
stop.think.rack.note: Most of what you see moves power, heat and data. The sums happen in a few chips on each board.
stop.think.board.q: Chips on this board do the same simple sums side by side. Is thinking just a great deal of adding?
stop.think.board.note: An AI model is mostly multiply-and-add, repeated billions of times.
stop.think.chip.q: No block on this chip understands your question. So where does the understanding live?
stop.think.chip.note: Each block does one narrow job: add, store, or move numbers.
stop.think.block.q: A memory cell here is a loop that holds one bit. Is remembering part of thinking, or something separate?
stop.think.block.note: Feed a circuit's output back into its input and it holds its state.
stop.think.gate.q: These switches make one kind of logic. Rewire the same switches and you get another. Does meaning come from the wiring?
stop.think.gate.note: The four switches here are identical. Only their connections differ.
stop.think.switch.q: This switch knows two states: on and off. How can on and off mean anything at all?
stop.think.switch.note: Meaning comes from an agreement about how to read a group of switches.
stop.think.atom.q: Down here there are only electrons moving through a crystal. At which depth did the thinking begin?
stop.think.atom.note: Nothing at this depth knows it is part of a computer.
stop.strange.chip.q: Almost every chip is made of silicon. What else could a chip be made of, and what would change?
stop.strange.chip.note: Silicon won because it is cheap, can be made extremely pure, and grows its own insulating layer.
stop.strange.gate.q: Dominoes, water and beams of light can each build this gate. What makes something a computer?
stop.strange.gate.note: Anything with two states, where one state can control another, can be wired into logic.
stop.strange.switch.q: What could replace the switch itself: a beam of light, a magnet's spin, a living cell?
stop.strange.switch.note: Every candidate so far beats the transistor at something and loses at something else.
stop.strange.atom.q: Could single atoms or molecules be the parts? What would we gain, and what would we lose?
stop.strange.atom.note: A working transistor has been made from a single atom in the laboratory.
stop.limit.rack.q: A rack like this can write, draw and compose. Is there anything it could never do?
stop.limit.rack.note: In 1936, before any chip existed, it was proved that some questions can never be settled by any machine.
stop.limit.chip.q: A chip is frozen the day it is made. What if it could keep changing?
stop.limit.chip.note: Most chips can never be rewired. A few kinds can.
stop.limit.chip.tried: chips that can be rewired after they are made
chips that learn while they run
stop.limit.gate.q: Some problems double in size with every item you add. Is "too hard" a law of nature, or a lack of ideas?
stop.limit.gate.note: For such problems, a faster chip only buys one more item.
stop.limit.gate.tried: quantum computers, for a few such problems
stop.limit.atom.q: Physics sets a smallest energy for erasing one bit. Is there a floor under all thinking?
stop.limit.atom.note: Today's chips use many thousands of times more than that minimum.
stop.fail.building.q: In a hall this size, something is always failing. Can a system be more reliable than its parts?
stop.fail.building.note: With hundreds of thousands of parts, rare faults happen every day.
stop.fail.board.q: One board here turns hundreds of watts into heat. Where does it all go?
stop.fail.board.note: Nearly all the electricity a chip uses leaves it as heat.
stop.fail.board.tried: chips that slow down when they get hot
stop.fail.chip.q: The design is exact. The arrival times are not. What does "on time" mean when every wire is a different length?
stop.fail.chip.note: If a signal arrives after the clock ticks, the chip reads the wrong value.
stop.fail.gate.q: No two of these gates come out identical. How do you design with parts you can't fully trust?
stop.fail.gate.note: Each is slightly faster or slower than its neighbour.
stop.fail.switch.q: A few atoms out of place change how this switch behaves. Is perfection even a meaningful goal?
stop.fail.switch.note: The thinnest layers here are only a few atoms thick.
stop.fail.atom.q: Walls this thin let electrons leak straight through. What do you do when the rules themselves change?
stop.fail.atom.note: At this size electrons behave partly like waves and can cross barriers that should stop them.
stop.idea.chip.q: Faster, cooler, smaller, cheaper: no chip gets all four. Who chose the trade-offs in this one?
stop.idea.chip.note: Every chip is a set of compromises made on purpose.
stop.idea.block.q: Nobody placed these cells by hand. If software arranged them, who is the designer?
stop.idea.block.note: People describe what the chip should do. Programs decide where the parts go.
stop.idea.block.tried: AI that places and wires chips
describing a chip in plain words
stop.idea.gate.q: A chip can't be patched after it is made. How sure is sure enough?
stop.idea.gate.note: Teams often spend more effort checking a design than creating it.
stop.idea.gate.tried: simulating the chip before building it
stop.make.chip.q: Chips are printed with light onto flat round wafers. Was that the only way it could have gone?
stop.make.chip.note: The newest machines print with light of wavelength 13.5 nanometres.
stop.make.switch.q: This shape is made by adding and carving away dozens of layers. Could it be grown instead?
stop.make.switch.note: A modern chip takes a thousand steps or more to make, and billions of switches are made at once.
stop.make.atom.q: What if atoms could be placed one at a time?
stop.make.atom.note: It has been done in the laboratory, slowly, with the tip of a microscope.
stop.know.chip.q: Two teams with the same tools get different chips. What does one know that the other doesn't?
stop.know.chip.note: Skill learned by doing is often impossible to put fully into words.
stop.know.switch.q: Getting this shape right took decades of trial and error. Can an AI learn what was never written down?
stop.know.switch.note: AI learns from recorded data. What was never recorded is the hard part.
stop.know.switch.tried: AI trained on factory sensor data
stop.open.chip.q: Many strangers can share one chip and split the cost. What should they build together?
stop.open.chip.note: Shared runs have put hundreds of small designs on one chip.
stop.open.block.q: Open blocks can be reused by anyone. What would a shared library of chip parts make possible?
stop.open.block.note: Software grew this way: people building on each other's pieces.
stop.open.block.tried: open cell libraries and design kits
stop.open.gate.q: An open design can be checked by anyone, and copied by anyone. Is that a strength or a risk?
stop.open.gate.note: A flaw in silicon can't be fixed after the chip is made.
stop.divide.building.q: Thousands of machines here act as one computer. Where does one computer end and the next begin?
stop.divide.building.note: A large AI model is trained across many racks at once.
stop.divide.rack.q: Most of this rack moves data and removes heat. Is that overhead, or is it the real work?
stop.divide.rack.note: Only a small part of the rack does the arithmetic.
stop.divide.board.q: A specialist chip sits at the centre with helpers all around. Who should be in charge?
stop.divide.board.note: The specialist is fast at one kind of sum and needs the others for everything else.
stop.divide.chip.q: A chip is a city of districts. What should be general, and what should be special?
stop.divide.chip.note: A general block can do any job passably. A special one does a single job far better.
stop.divide.chip.tried: chiplets: small chips joined in one package
stop.divide.block.q: Memory and logic sit apart, joined by busy wires. Was separating them a mistake?
stop.divide.block.note: Fetching a number can cost more energy than computing with it.
stop.divide.block.tried: stacking memory on top of logic
stop.life.building.q: A hall like this can use as much power as a town. A brain runs on about 20 watts. What is the brain doing differently?
stop.life.building.note: Much of a data centre's power ends up as heat that has to be carried away.
stop.life.block.q: Brain cells stay quiet until something changes. What if these cells did too?
stop.life.block.note: Most chip circuits are driven by a clock whether or not there is anything new to do.
stop.life.switch.q: A synapse stores and computes in the same place. What would a switch like that be?
stop.life.switch.note: In a brain, the connections that hold memories are the ones that do the computing.
stop.life.atom.q: Life builds with atoms cheaply, at room temperature. What could chemistry teach a factory?
stop.life.atom.note: A cell assembles complex molecular machines without a clean room.
stop.scale.building.q: Each answer costs less energy every year, yet we ask for ever more. Can the planet afford the answers we want?
stop.scale.building.note: Nearly all the electricity a hall like this uses leaves it as heat.
stop.scale.chip.q: Shrinking is slowing. What should double next: switches, usefulness, or something nobody measures yet?
stop.scale.chip.note: For decades the number of switches on the best chips doubled about every two years.
stop.scale.switch.q: Flat, then fins, then sheets. What comes after the sheet, and can anything keep doubling forever?
stop.scale.switch.note: Each new shape gave the gate a firmer grip on the channel, so it could shrink again.
stop.scale.switch.tried: stacking the two kinds of switch on top of each other
stop.scale.atom.q: When a channel is a few dozen atoms long, what is left to shrink?
stop.scale.atom.note: The pattern of a silicon crystal repeats about every half a nanometre.

depth.phone.name: Phone
depth.phone.see: A phone with its back opened: the main board, the battery that has to last the day, the camera.
depth.phoneboard.name: Board
depth.phoneboard.see: The phone's main board, a few centimetres across, packed with parts. There is no fan.
depth.soc.name: Chip
depth.soc.see: The phone's chip: processor cores, graphics, an AI unit and a camera unit, each in its own district.
depth.car.name: Car
depth.car.see: An electric car, roof and near side cut away: control units everywhere, joined by wires, with sensors looking out. The one in the footwell has its lid off.
depth.ecu.name: Control unit
depth.ecu.see: One control unit, the lid off: a small chip that decides, and big parts that switch real power.
depth.mcu.name: Chip
depth.mcu.see: A microcontroller, a few millimetres across: two small cores, the memory that keeps its program, and its links to the world.
stop.life.phone.q: Your brain runs all day on about the power of a dim light bulb. Your phone needs charging every night. What would a chip that sips, rather than gulps, look like?
stop.life.phone.note: Most of the time a phone's chip is waiting. How little it spends while waiting decides how long the battery lasts.
stop.life.phone.tried: Big and little cores: little ones for small jobs
Switching off every part not in use, many times a second
stop.divide.phone.q: Your phone answers some questions itself and sends others far away. Which work should stay in your hand?
stop.divide.phone.note: Phones now carry a unit made just for AI, so more of the thinking can happen without the network.
stop.divide.phone.tried: Small AI models that run on the phone
Splitting one task between the phone and the cloud
stop.know.phone.q: A phone photo is shaped by people who looked at thousands of pictures and said "that looks right". Can taste be written down?
stop.know.phone.note: The colours and tones a camera produces are tuned by eye, by teams who know what a good picture feels like.
stop.fail.phoneboard.q: All this is packed into a few square centimetres, with no fan. Where does the heat go?
stop.fail.phoneboard.note: When a phone gets too hot, it slows its own chip down to protect itself, and you.
stop.scale.phoneboard.q: Here the memory sits right on top of the processor. When you can't go smaller, do you go up?
stop.scale.phoneboard.note: Stacking shortens the distance data has to travel, which saves time and energy.
stop.open.phoneboard.q: The radio rules every phone follows are shared and public, yet only a few companies make the modem. Why?
stop.open.phoneboard.note: Writing a standard down is not the same as building something that works with every network in the world.
stop.divide.soc.q: This chip has a district just for photos and one just for AI. When does a job earn its own district?
stop.divide.soc.note: A special district costs space on the chip, and pays it back by doing its one job with far less energy.
stop.think.soc.q: Your camera finds faces before you press the button. Which part of this chip is doing that?
stop.think.soc.note: An AI unit does a great many small multiplications at once, spending very little energy on each.
stop.idea.soc.q: The processor cores here were probably designed by another company. Can a chip be built mostly from other people's blocks?
stop.idea.soc.note: Most phone chips combine licensed designs with parts their makers design themselves.
stop.idea.soc.tried: Licensing processor designs from one company
Open RISC-V designs anyone can use and change
stop.scale.soc.q: Phone chips are often the first made in each new factory process. Why phones?
stop.scale.soc.note: Phones sell in such numbers that they help pay for the newest, most expensive factories.
stop.fail.car.q: A car's chips must work in freezing winters and beside a hot engine, for many years. How do you design for weather you can't predict?
stop.fail.car.note: Car chips are tested at temperature extremes far beyond what a phone ever meets.
stop.divide.car.q: A car can have dozens of small computers, one for each job. Should it have a few big ones instead?
stop.divide.car.note: Every small computer brings its own wires, and wiring has become one of the heaviest parts of a car.
stop.know.car.q: A few years ago, car factories stopped because small, cheap chips ran out. How can a part that costs so little stop so much?
stop.know.car.note: Many car chips are made in older factory processes, in factories qualified years ago, which cannot simply be swapped.
stop.life.car.q: A car drives by watching through cameras and radar. Animals see with far less energy. What could chips learn from eyes?
stop.life.car.note: An eye does not send every point of light to the brain; much of the work happens before the signal leaves it.
stop.life.car.tried: Cameras that report only what changes, like an eye
Chips that compute right where the image is captured
stop.fail.ecu.q: This unit works the brakes. If one chip makes one wrong move, a life is at risk. How do you trust a chip with a life?
stop.fail.ecu.note: Safety chips assume that something will go wrong, and are built to notice it in time.
stop.fail.ecu.tried: Two cores running the same work in step, compared every moment
Self-tests every time the car starts
Safety standards that trace every requirement to a test
stop.open.ecu.q: Car makers often write their own software for chips they buy from others. What if the software were shared?
stop.open.ecu.note: More car makers now build on shared foundations, and compete on what they build on top.
stop.divide.ecu.q: The small chip decides; the big parts beside it switch the current. Where does thinking end and power begin?
stop.divide.ecu.note: Power parts are often made from different materials, such as silicon carbide, which handle high voltage and heat.
stop.think.mcu.q: This chip runs one small program, over and over, for the whole life of the car. Is that thinking?
stop.think.mcu.note: Most of the world's chips are small controllers like this one, not big processors.
stop.scale.mcu.q: This chip is made on purpose in an older process. When is smaller not better?
stop.scale.mcu.note: Memory that keeps its contents with the power off, like this flash, is hard to shrink, and older processes are proven over years.
stop.make.mcu.q: Chips like this are made by the billion and cost very little. What does it take to make something that cheap, that reliable?
stop.make.mcu.note: Making it cheap and making it reliable pull in different directions, and both have to win.

case.sdc.t: Cores that quietly compute wrong answers
case.sdc.what: Google and Meta found processors in their data centres that now and then gave wrong results, with no crash and no warning.
case.sdc.why: Tiny manufacturing flaws that the factory test missed, some showing up only with certain instructions, at certain temperatures, or after some ageing. Rare in one chip, but a data centre has millions of cores.
case.sdc.after: Large data centres now keep testing chips while they work, and retire the bad ones.
case.sdc.src: Meta: Detecting silent data corruptions in the wild (2022)
case.raptor.what: Owners of high-end Intel desktop processors reported crashes that began after months of use and got worse.
case.raptor.why: A clock circuit in each core aged faster under high voltage and heat, and the boards were asking for more voltage than it could take over time.
case.raptor.after: Updates capped the voltage and the warranty grew by two years. An update can stop further ageing, but it cannot undo the damage already done.
case.raptor.src: Intel: root cause of the instability (September 2024)
case.p3.what: Weeks after launch, reviewers found that Intel's fastest Pentium III crashed in some heavy jobs. Intel reproduced the problem and recalled the chip.
case.p3.why: Pushed to that speed, some chips had too little room for error in their timing. Most worked; the ones at the edge did not.
case.p3.after: A chip's speed rating must hold for the slowest chip, the hottest day and the weakest power supply, not the average. Chips are now sorted by tested speed and sold with a safety margin.
case.spectre.what: Researchers showed that almost every fast processor of the time could be tricked into leaking secrets, such as passwords, from other programs.
case.spectre.why: To run faster, processors guess ahead and do work before they know it is needed. That worked exactly as designed; nobody had imagined an attacker reading the faint traces those guesses leave behind.
case.spectre.after: Patches first, then changes in new chips. Security became a design goal next to speed, energy and cost.
case.spectre.src: Meltdown and Spectre (Graz University of Technology and others)
case.fdiv.t: The Pentium that could not divide
case.fdiv.what: A mathematics professor noticed that Intel's new Pentium sometimes gave wrong answers when dividing. The error was rare: about one in nine billion random divisions, by one estimate.
case.fdiv.why: Five entries were missing from a table inside the divider. The chip did exactly what its design said; the design was wrong, and the tests never tried those numbers.
case.fdiv.after: Intel replaced the chips. Chipmakers turned to formal verification: proving with mathematics that a circuit is right for every input, not only for the inputs someone thought to test.
case.cougar.what: Soon after launch, Intel found that a support chip for its new processors had disk ports that would wear out. New chips passed every test.
case.cougar.why: A design error put one circuit under too much stress, so it would fail after years of use. Nothing was wrong on the first day, which is why the factory test could not see it.
case.cougar.after: Intel stopped shipping, fixed the chip and replaced the old ones. Checking how every circuit ages over its whole life is now a standard step before a design goes to the factory.
case.vote.what: In a Belgian election, one candidate received more votes than were possible. A recount found 4,096 votes too many.
case.vote.why: 4,096 is exactly 2 to the power of 12: a single bit in memory had flipped from 0 to 1. A particle from space is the suspected cause, never proven.
case.vote.after: It became the classic example of a soft error, and of why memory that corrects its own errors belongs wherever a wrong number matters: servers, cars, aircraft, voting machines.

depth.scanner.name: Machine
depth.scanner.see: The machine that prints with light: light made from tin, bounced off mirrors and a mask onto the wafer.
depth.wafer.name: Wafer
depth.wafer.see: One wafer of your chips. Specks land at random, and every chip a speck touches is lost.
depth.die.name: Chip
depth.die.see: One of your chips, still on the wafer: test needles touch its pads before it is cut out.
stop.make.scanner.q: To get light short enough, this machine fires a laser at tiny drops of molten tin, over and over every second. Is this the simplest way to print a chip?
stop.make.scanner.note: Air swallows this light, so its whole path runs through a vacuum, bouncing off mirrors instead of passing through lenses.
stop.scale.scanner.q: Shorter light prints smaller details. What happens when the light can't get any shorter?
stop.scale.scanner.note: The newest machines gather the light with larger mirrors instead, to print finer still.
stop.scale.scanner.tried: Larger mirrors that gather more of the light
Printing one layer in several passes
stop.open.scanner.q: Every machine like this comes from a single maker. What does it mean when a whole industry depends on one machine?
stop.open.scanner.note: It took decades, and parts from many countries, to make it work.
stop.fail.wafer.q: Specks land at random. Why does a bigger chip come out broken more often?
stop.fail.wafer.note: A speck ruins only the chip it lands on, so the bigger each chip, the more each speck costs.
stop.make.wafer.q: Hundreds of square chips are made at once on a round disc. Why round?
stop.make.wafer.note: Wafers are sliced from a crystal that grows as a round rod, and the chips cut off at the edge are wasted.
stop.idea.die.q: This pattern began as someone's idea. How many people and machines did it pass through to get here?
stop.idea.die.note: Designing a chip for the newest process now costs more than most companies can spend.
stop.make.die.q: Next it is cut out, sealed in a package and wired to the world. Is the package becoming as important as the chip?
stop.make.die.note: Packages now join several chips and stacks of memory close enough to act almost as one.
stop.make.die.tried: Stacking chips on top of each other
Joining chips with light instead of wires
chip.size.label: Chip size
chip.size.notice: A bigger chip holds more, but fewer fit on a wafer and more of them are hit. Where would you stop?

ui.howLine: Swipe, scroll sideways or use the arrow keys to move along the line. Stop at a machine to watch your wafer go through it, step by numbered step.
depth.crystal.name: Crystal
depth.crystal.see: Every chip starts as sand. It is purified, melted, and pulled up slowly as one perfect crystal.
depth.slice.name: Wafers
depth.slice.see: The crystal is sawn into thin discs and polished flatter than almost anything else people make. Here your wafer begins its journey.
depth.pkg.name: Package
depth.pkg.see: In another plant, the wafer is cut into chips. Each good one is placed on its package, often with memory beside it, and closed with a lid.
depth.ship.name: Out
depth.ship.see: A last test, then out into the world: into a data centre, a phone or a car.
stop.make.crystal.q: Every chip starts as sand, melted and pulled up as one perfect crystal. Why must the whole crystal be a single, unbroken pattern?
stop.make.crystal.note: A row of atoms out of place here would spoil every chip cut from that part of the crystal.
stop.know.crystal.q: Pulling a crystal this pure is slow and delicate. How much of it depends on people who have done it for years?
stop.know.crystal.note: Only a few companies in the world make most of the wafers chips are built on.
stop.strange.crystal.q: Silicon for chips is among the purest materials people make. Does it have to be?
stop.strange.crystal.note: Solar cells are made of silicon too, at a purity a chip could never work with.
stop.make.slice.q: A wire saw cuts the crystal into discs thinner than a coin. What is lost in every cut?
stop.make.slice.note: Much of the crystal turns to dust in the saw.
stop.scale.slice.q: Wafers grew from the size of a coin to the size of a dinner plate. Why stop there?
stop.scale.slice.note: A move to even larger wafers was planned for years, then shelved: every machine in every factory would have had to change.
stop.make.pkg.q: The chip is flipped face down and joined to its package by tiny solder bumps. Why face down?
stop.make.pkg.note: Face down, every part of the chip can connect straight to the package, not only its edges.
stop.divide.pkg.q: Here memory sits right beside the processor, in one package. Where should one chip end and the next begin?
stop.divide.pkg.note: Placing memory this close shortens the wires data has to travel.
stop.divide.pkg.tried: Stacking memory in towers beside the processor
Small chips side by side on a shared base, working as one
stop.fail.pkg.q: Chip and package warm up and grow by different amounts. How do you stop them tearing apart?
stop.fail.pkg.note: Materials are chosen to expand at nearly the same rate as the chip.
stop.fail.ship.q: Every packaged chip is tested once more before it leaves. Who decides what counts as good enough?
stop.fail.ship.note: Chips that run slower or hotter are often sold as a cheaper model instead of being thrown away.
stop.open.ship.q: The same factory makes chips for rival companies. What does a factory owe the companies it makes chips for?
stop.open.ship.note: Many chip companies design chips but never make them; a few factories make chips for all of them.
stop.divide.ship.q: One chip goes into a data centre, another into a phone, another into a car. Should they have been made differently from the start?
stop.divide.ship.note: Car chips are often made in older processes, phone chips in the newest, and data centre chips as large as a chip can be.

what.building.racks: Rows of tall cabinets full of computers; this is where the work is done.
what.building.cooling: Pumps and fans that carry the heat away, because every bit of electricity the chips use ends up as heat.
what.building.power: Brings in electricity from the grid and steadies it, with batteries ready if the supply drops.
what.rack.servers: Each shelf is one computer, built around a few large chips.
what.rack.switch: Connects the servers to each other and to the rest of the hall, so many machines can work as one.
what.rack.power: Turns the hall's electricity into the steady low voltage the boards need.
what.rack.cooling: Liquid flows in cold and out warm, carrying heat away from the chips.
what.board.bigchip: The chip that does the calculating: thousands of small units working at once.
what.board.memory: Holds the numbers the chip is working on, as close to it as possible.
what.board.power: Turns the board's supply into the very low, very steady voltage the chip needs.
what.board.traces: Copper lines that carry data between the memory and the chip.
what.board.connectors: Where the board plugs into the server, for power and for data.
what.chip.cores: Blocks that do the work: each fetches instructions and numbers, calculates, and passes results on.
what.chip.cache: Fast memory on the chip itself, so the cores rarely wait for the slower memory outside.
what.chip.io: The chip's doors: circuits that send and receive signals to and from everything around it.
what.chip.clock: Wires carrying the tick that keeps every part of the chip in step.
what.phone.board: The main board: the phone's chip, memory, radio and power chips, packed together.
what.phone.battery: Stores the energy for the whole day; how slowly the chip spends it decides how long it lasts.
what.phone.camera: Lenses and light sensors; much of a photo is then computed by the chip.
what.phone.antenna: Parts of the frame act as antennas, sending and receiving radio waves.
what.phoneboard.soc: The phone's chip, with its memory stacked on top of it.
what.phoneboard.pmic: The power chip: hands out the battery's energy, a different voltage to each part.
what.phoneboard.modem: Turns data into radio signals and back, following the rules every network shares.
what.phoneboard.storage: Keeps your photos, apps and messages when the power is off.
what.soc.cpu: General cores: big ones for heavy work, small ones that sip energy for light work.
what.soc.gpu: Many small, identical cores that draw images, all at once.
what.soc.npu: Built for the multiplications AI needs: many at a time, using little energy.
what.soc.isp: Turns the camera sensor's raw signal into a picture: colour, sharpness, noise.
what.soc.cache: Memory every district shares, so they can pass work to each other quickly.
what.car.controllers: Small computers, each in charge of one job: brakes, engine, windows, lights.
what.car.wiring: Cables that carry power and messages between the control units.
what.car.sensors: Cameras and radar that watch the road and feed the computers.
what.car.wheels: What the computers finally move: through brakes, steering and motors.
what.ecu.mcu: The small chip that makes the decisions, running one program over and over.
what.ecu.connector: Where the unit plugs into the car's wiring, for power, sensors and messages.
what.ecu.drivers: Large switches that turn real current on and off, on the small chip's command.
what.mcu.cores: Two small cores running the same work in step, so a mistake shows up as a difference.
what.mcu.flash: Keeps the program even when the car is switched off.
what.mcu.sram: Fast memory for the numbers the program is working on right now.
what.mcu.periph: Converts signals from sensors into numbers, talks to the car's network, keeps time.
what.crystal.sand: Quartz sand: silicon joined to oxygen, the raw material of every chip.
what.crystal.furnace: Melts purified silicon and keeps it at a steady heat for many hours.
what.crystal.melt: Molten silicon, waiting to be pulled up as a crystal.
what.crystal.ingot: A single crystal, its atoms in one unbroken pattern, pulled up slowly while it turns.
what.slice.ingot: The crystal, ready to be cut into wafers.
what.slice.saw: Fine wires running fast through the crystal, cutting many wafers at once.
what.slice.wafers: Thin discs of crystal; every chip will be built on one.
what.slice.polish: A turning pad polishes each wafer until its surface is almost perfectly flat.
what.pkg.saw: A thin, turning blade cuts the wafer apart, chip by chip.
what.pkg.substrate: The package's base: layers of wiring that spread the chip's connections out to the board.
what.pkg.bumps: Tiny drops of solder that join the chip to the package, face down.
what.pkg.die: The chip itself, flipped so its whole face can connect.
what.pkg.memory: Memory chips stacked in towers right beside the processor.
what.pkg.lid: Protects the chip and carries its heat away.
what.ship.trays: Every packaged chip is tested once more; the slower ones may be sold as a cheaper model.
what.ship.boxes: Packed and sent to the companies that build the final products.
what.ship.datacentre: Where the largest chips go: into servers in a data centre.
what.ship.phone: Where the most energy-thrifty chips go: into phones.
what.ship.car: Where the toughest chips go: into cars, for many years of heat and cold.
what.scanner.source: Makes light so short it is close to X-rays, by hitting drops of tin with a laser.
what.scanner.mirrors: Polished mirrors guide the light, because this light is swallowed by glass.
what.scanner.mask: Holds the pattern of one layer, like a stencil, magnified.
what.scanner.stage: Moves the wafer under the light with astonishing precision, exposing one chip after another.
what.wafer.dies: The chips on this wafer, all made at once, all the same.
what.wafer.defects: Specks that landed during making; each ruins the chip it falls on.
what.die.cores: Your chip's cores, the same at every step down to here.
what.die.pads: Small metal squares where the chip connects to the outside world.
what.die.probes: Needles that touch the pads to test the chip before it is cut out.
what.die.scribe: The lane between chips, where the saw will cut.
what.block.cells: Tiny standard building blocks, each a small logic circuit, lined up in rows.
what.block.sram: A grid of memory cells, each holding one bit.
what.block.wires: Metal lines on many levels above the cells, connecting them.
what.gate.gates: Strips of material that switch the channels under them on and off.
what.gate.diff: Where current flows when a gate lets it.
what.gate.metal: Wires that carry the inputs in and the result out.
what.switch.gate: Wraps around the sheets; its voltage decides whether current can flow.
what.switch.channel: Thin sheets of silicon the current flows through.
what.switch.oxide: A very thin insulating skin between the gate and the sheets.
what.atom.lattice: Silicon atoms, each joined to four neighbours in a regular pattern.
what.atom.dopant: An atom of another element, added on purpose to change how easily current flows.
what.atom.electrons: The moving charges that carry the current.
what.atom.boundary: An insulating layer; when it is only a few atoms thick, electrons can slip through.

chal.title: Challenge
chal.fast.goal: Make your chip tick twice as fast, with no signal arriving late.
chal.fast.hint: The clock alone can't do it: the slowest signal needs faster switches. Look for where the switch size changes.
chal.battery.goal: Make the phone's battery last one and a half times as long, at full speed, still with at least 12 cores.
chal.battery.hint: A smaller chip uses less energy but holds fewer cores. What could fit the cores back in?
chal.cores.goal: Give your chip at least 20 cores, while each good chip costs no more than 0.7 times the starting chip's.
chal.cores.hint: Cores come from smaller switches or from a bigger chip. One of them is kind to the wafer; the other is not.
chal.quick.goal: Get your chip through the factory in about 50 days or fewer, still with at least 12 cores.
chal.quick.hint: Older, larger switches need fewer layers. What else could make room for cores?
stop.make.clean.q: This whole factory exists to keep dust away from wafers. If we started today, would we still build it this way?
stop.make.clean.note: A speck far smaller than a hair can ruin a chip, so the air inside is kept far cleaner than an operating theatre's.
stop.make.clean.tried: Keeping only each wafer's sealed box clean, not the whole room
Small factories that fit in one room and make chips in small batches
stop.scale.clean.q: Each new factory for the newest chips costs more than the last. Can that cost keep rising faster than chips earn?
stop.scale.clean.note: Only a few companies in the world can still afford to build one.
stop.open.clean.q: Only a handful of companies can make the newest chips. What would change if making chips were as open as writing software?
stop.open.clean.note: Factories for older processes make chips for anyone who sends a design, and shared runs now cost about as much as a used car.
stop.know.etch.q: Robots carry the wafers, yet the factory depends on people who can tell when a machine is not quite right. Can that be written down?
stop.know.etch.note: Starting a new factory often means bringing in experienced people from an old one.
stop.fail.etch.q: Wafers are checked for flaws again and again along the way. How many checks are enough, when each one costs time?
stop.fail.etch.note: Catching a flaw early saves every step that would have come after it.
stop.divide.wires.q: Hundreds of machines each do one kind of step, and a wafer visits many of them many times. Who decides the order?
stop.divide.wires.note: Scheduling software routes every wafer, and one slow machine can hold up the whole factory.
stop.make.wires.q: Every layer goes round the same loop, and a chip needs dozens of layers. Must a chip be made one layer at a time?
stop.make.wires.note: One lap prints the pattern of a single layer; the wafer then goes back to cleaning for the next.
stop.fail.test.q: Needles test every chip before the wafer is cut. What can a test never catch?
stop.fail.test.note: A test checks only what someone thought to check.
stop.divide.test.q: Small chips come out good more often, as the map shows. Should one big chip be split into several small ones that work together?
stop.divide.test.note: Joining small chips in one package trades a little speed between them for many more good chips.
stop.divide.test.tried: Chiplets: several small chips side by side in one package
One giant chip that fills a whole wafer, built to work around its flaws

depth.clean.name: Clean
depth.clean.see: Into the factory. Before every layer, the wafer is washed until not a speck is left.
depth.deposit.name: Deposit
depth.deposit.see: A thin new film is laid over the whole wafer, from gases that react on its hot surface.
depth.print.name: Print
depth.print.see: Three machines joined as one: a light-sensitive layer is coated on, a pattern is printed into it with light, and the parts the light touched are washed away.
depth.etch.name: Etch
depth.etch.see: Plasma cuts the film away wherever the pattern left it uncovered, straight down.
depth.implant.name: Implant
depth.implant.see: Atoms of another element are shot into the silicon where it is open, then a flash of heat heals the crystal around them.
depth.wires.name: Wires
depth.wires.see: Copper fills the cut trenches and is polished flat. Then the wafer goes back round the loop for the next layer.
depth.test.name: Test
depth.test.see: Needles touch every chip on the wafer. The map shows which are good, which depends on your chip's size.
what.clean.tool: Washes wafers one at a time with ultrapure water and chemicals, in spinning chambers behind robots.
what.deposit.tool: A sealed chamber where gases react on the hot wafer and leave a thin film.
what.deposit.gas: Bring in the gases the film is made from, in precise amounts.
what.deposit.heater: Keeps the wafer hot enough for the gases to react on its surface.
what.print.coat: Spins the wafer fast to spread a light-sensitive layer thinner than a soap bubble.
what.print.scanner: Shines light through a mask to print one layer's pattern, chip after chip across the wafer.
what.print.develop: Washes away the parts of the layer the light touched, leaving the pattern.
what.print.light: Light so short it is close to X-rays, carrying the pattern down to the wafer.
what.print.mask: Holds the pattern of one layer, like a stencil.
what.etch.tool: Fills with plasma and cuts the film where the pattern left it open.
what.etch.plasma: A glowing gas of charged particles, pulled straight down to cut straight down.
what.etch.people: Watches and tunes the machines; much of what keeps them right is know-how.
what.implant.tool: Fires a beam of atoms into the open parts of the wafer.
what.implant.beam: Atoms of another element, given a charge and sped up to strike the silicon.
what.implant.magnet: Bends the beam so that only the wanted kind of atom reaches the wafer.
what.implant.heater: Heats the wafer for a moment so the crystal heals around the new atoms.
what.wires.plating: Copper grows into the cut trenches, like plating a spoon.
what.wires.polish: A turning pad polishes the copper away until only the trenches are filled, perfectly flat.
what.wires.loop: The wafer returns to cleaning for the next layer, and the next, until all are done.
what.test.prober: Moves the wafer under a card of needles, touching one chip after another.
what.test.needles: Touch the chip's pads to send signals in and read the answers.
what.test.map: Every chip on your wafer: good ones green, the ones a speck ruined red.
stop.idea.deposit.q: Some films are laid down one layer of atoms at a time. If we can build that precisely, what else could we build?
stop.idea.deposit.note: Two gases take turns, and each turn leaves exactly one layer of atoms.
stop.strange.deposit.q: Every layer here is a different material, chosen for one job: to conduct, to insulate, to block. Could a chip be built from entirely different materials?
stop.strange.deposit.note: Chips already use dozens of elements, far beyond silicon: copper, cobalt, tungsten, hafnium and more.
stop.fail.print.q: Each layer's pattern has to line up with the one below, to within a few atoms. What happens when it doesn't?
stop.fail.print.note: The machine measures the wafer's position again and again while it prints, and corrects it as it goes.
stop.scale.print.q: Printing is the slowest and costliest step, so whole factories are planned around it. What would change if printing were cheap?
stop.scale.print.note: Factories are laid out so the printing machines are never left waiting.
stop.make.etch.q: Plasma cuts trenches far deeper than they are wide, straight down. How do you cut only downward?
stop.make.etch.note: Charged particles are pulled straight down by an electric field, so they hit the bottom of the trench, not its walls.
stop.make.implant.q: Atoms of another element are fired into the silicon on purpose. Why would you want impurities?
stop.make.implant.note: A few added atoms change how easily current flows; that is what makes a switch possible.
stop.fail.implant.q: The beam knocks the crystal out of place; a flash of heat repairs it. How much damage can a crystal forgive?
stop.fail.implant.note: Heating for only a moment lets the atoms settle back into their pattern without the added ones wandering away.

what.clean.chamber: The wafer spins while a moving arm sprays it, then it is rinsed and spun dry.
what.handle.pod: A sealed box with slots for a stack of wafers. It opens only against a machine's door, so the wafers never meet the room's air.
what.handle.efem: A robot arm in a small, extra-clean room at the front of the machine. It lifts wafers out of the pod by their underside.
what.handle.lock: A small room with a door on each side. Air is pumped out before the inner door opens, so the vacuum inside the machine is never broken.
what.handle.xfer: A second robot inside the machine, carrying the wafer to whichever chamber is free. In machines that work in vacuum, it works in vacuum too.
what.handle.shelf: Where the front robot leaves the wafer for the robot inside the machine.
what.handle.dock: Where crates of pods arrive from another plant, often from another country.
what.handle.tray: After packaging, chips travel in trays, one pocket each.
handle.arrive: Docking Lowered from the track, the sealed pod lands on the machine's door. It opens only against the machine, so the wafer never meets the room's air.
handle.take: Front robot A robot arm reaches into the pod and lifts the wafer out from below, in air kept even cleaner than the room's.
handle.lock: Airlock The outer door closes behind the wafer and pumps pull the air out. Only then does the inner door open, onto the vacuum.
handle.move: Inner robot A second robot, working in the vacuum, carries the wafer to a chamber that is free.
handle.handoff: Hand-off The front robot leaves the wafer on a shelf, where a robot inside the machine picks it up.
handle.inside: Inner robot The robot inside the machine carries the wafer to a chamber that is free.
handle.back: Back the same way Robot to robot, and back into the pod. Every move is a chance to pick up a speck, so moves are few and quick.
handle.done: Done here The pod closes and is lifted back to the track. Move along the line to follow it to the next machine.
handle.travel: On the track Pods ride an overhead track from machine to machine. Much of a wafer's time in the factory is spent travelling and waiting its turn, not being worked on.
handle.ship: To another plant Between plants, pods and trays travel packed in crates, by truck or by plane, often to another country.
handle.ingot: To the saw The finished crystal is ground perfectly round and taken to be sliced.
handle.into: Into the pod A robot slides your finished wafer into a sealed pod. From here on it is carried by machines, never touched by hand.
handle.start: The journey starts The pod leaves for the chip factory, which is often in another place.
handle.loop: Round again Back to the start of the loop for the next layer. Your chip goes round about {layers} times.
handle.packed: Into a tray With its lid on, your finished chip is placed in a tray, to leave for its last test.
handle.trays: In trays Finished chips arrive in trays, one pocket each, to be tested one last time.
handle.out: Out Packed and labelled, the chips leave for the companies that build them into data centres, phones and cars.
proc.crystal.sand: Sand Silicon comes from quartz sand. It is purified until almost nothing but silicon is left.
proc.crystal.melt: Melt The pure silicon is melted in a quartz bowl, hotter than lava.
proc.crystal.pull: Pull A small seed crystal dips into the melt and is drawn slowly up, turning. Silicon freezes onto it as one perfect crystal, over a day or more.
proc.slice.saw: Saw Wires coated with diamond cut the crystal into hundreds of thin slices at once.
proc.slice.polish: Polish Each slice is ground and polished until it is flatter than almost anything people make: this is your wafer.
proc.clean: Wash The wafer spins while jets of ultrapure water and chemicals wash away specks and leftovers. Every new layer starts here.
proc.deposit: New film In the hot chamber, gases react on the wafer and leave a film over its whole surface, far thinner than a soap bubble.
proc.print.coat: Coat A drop of light-sensitive liquid is spun out into an even layer: it changes wherever light falls on it.
proc.print.expose: Print Light shines through the mask, the pattern of one layer, and lenses shrink it onto the wafer, one patch after another.
proc.print.develop: Develop A liquid washes away the parts the light touched. What is left is a stencil for the next machine.
proc.etch: Etch In vacuum, a glowing gas of charged particles (plasma) cuts the film straight down wherever the stencil leaves it bare. Then the stencil is stripped away.
proc.implant.beam: Implant Atoms of another element are given a charge, sped up, sorted by a magnet and shot into the bare silicon. They change how it conducts.
proc.implant.heat: Heal A flash of heat, far shorter than a second, lets the shaken crystal settle and the new atoms take their places.
proc.wires.plate: Copper In a bath, an electric current grows copper into every cut, and over everything else too.
proc.wires.polish: Polish flat Pressed onto a turning pad with a fine slurry, the extra copper is polished away. Copper is left only in the cuts: wires.
proc.test: Test A card of fine needles touches each chip in turn and runs it. The map fills in: green works, red does not.
proc.pkg.saw: Cut A thin turning blade, or a laser, cuts the wafer into separate chips.
proc.pkg.pick: Pick A head picks up a chip the map marked good, and flips it face down.
proc.pkg.bond: Join Tiny solder bumps join the chip to its package base, which carries signals and power out to the board.
proc.ship.test: Last test Pressed into a socket, each packaged chip is tested once more, often hot and cold.
proc.ship.pack: Pack Chips are sorted by how fast they run and packed for the companies that ordered them.
slice.title: your wafer, cut open
what.handle.track: Carries sealed boxes of wafers from machine to machine, all through the factory.
what.handle.filters: Filters across the whole ceiling push clean air down, carrying dust away from the wafers.
lens.title: under the lens: your wafer
lens.crystal: Silicon atoms from the melt settle onto the crystal, each one in line with the atoms below it. One mistake in the rows and the crystal is no good.
lens.polish: Slurry and a turning pad grind the cut surface down until it is flat and smooth as a mirror.
lens.clean: Liquids wash over the surface and carry the specks away. A speck left here can ruin the chip printed over it.
lens.deposit: Gas flows over the hot wafer and leaves a film behind, a few atoms at a time, evenly everywhere.
lens.coat: A drop of light-sensitive liquid is spun out into an even stencil layer over the film.
lens.expose: Light passes only through the mask's openings. Where it lands, the stencil changes.
lens.develop: A liquid washes away the stencil where the light changed it, leaving openings down to the film.
lens.etch: Ions in the plasma strike straight down. They cut the film only where the stencil is open.
lens.implant: Atoms of another element are fired into the silicon through the openings. They change how it carries current.
lens.heat: A flash of heat lets the new atoms settle into the silicon's rows, where they can do their work.
lens.plate: Copper from the bath grows over everything, filling every cut.
lens.cmp: The pad polishes the copper back until it is left only in the cuts: these are the wires.
lens.probe: A needle touches each chip's pads, and the test head runs the chip for a moment.
lens.dice: The wafer is cut apart. Each good chip gets small balls of solder on its face.
lens.bond: The chip goes face down onto its package base. Heat melts the solder and joins them.
lens.final: In its package, the chip is tested again, hot and then cold, as it will be used.

site.sv.name: Silicon Valley
site.sv.what: Chip design, and the software chips are designed with. Many of the world's chips are specified and designed here, and several of the biggest makers of fab tools are based nearby.
site.sv.who: Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Synopsys, Cadence, Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA
site.sd.name: San Diego
site.sd.what: Qualcomm designs the chips inside many of the world's phones here.
site.sea.name: Seattle
site.sea.what: Home of two of the largest cloud companies, which now design their own chips for their data centres.
site.phx.name: Phoenix
site.phx.what: A new cluster of chip fabs: TSMC's fabs in Arizona and Intel's newest fab, with advanced packaging planned nearby.
site.abi.name: Texas
site.abi.what: Large new data centres for AI, where racks of accelerators are switched on and run for years.
site.spr.name: Spruce Pine
site.spr.what: A small town in North Carolina that mines most of the world's ultra-pure quartz, used for the crucibles silicon crystals are grown in.
site.gdl.name: Guadalajara
site.gdl.what: Servers and racks are assembled here, close to customers in the United States.
site.cam.name: Cambridge

site.vel.name: Veldhoven

site.obk.name: Oberkochen

site.mun.name: Munich
site.mun.what: Infineon, one of the largest makers of chips for cars and power, has its headquarters here, and Siltronic makes silicon wafers.
site.stu.name: Stuttgart

site.stu.who: Bosch; Mercedes-Benz and Porsche build cars here

site.isr.name: Israel
site.isr.what: Chip design centres for many companies, and Intel's fab at Kiryat Gat.
site.btu.name: Baotou

site.sha.what: China's chip hub: SMIC, its largest foundry, and many chip design companies, including some that design phone chips.
site.zz.name: Zhengzhou
site.zz.what: One of the largest phone factories in the world, where phones are put together from chips made elsewhere.
site.ich.name: Icheon
site.ich.what: South of Seoul, Samsung and SK hynix make much of the world's memory, including the stacked memory AI chips use. Samsung also makes chips for other companies.
site.tky.name: Tokyo
site.tky.what: Japan's makers of wafers, chemicals and tools: much of the world's silicon wafers and photoresist, coaters, testers, and the film inside high-end packages. Renesas, a large maker of car chips, is based here.
site.tky.who: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, Tokyo Electron, Advantest, JSR, Tokyo Ohka, Ajinomoto, Renesas
site.naka.name: Naka
site.naka.what: A Renesas fab that makes chips for cars. A fire here in March 2021 stopped a line for about a month, while carmakers were already short of chips.
site.kum.name: Kumamoto
site.kum.what: TSMC's joint venture with Sony and Denso has made chips here since 2024, and a second fab is being built.
site.hsc.name: Hsinchu
site.hsc.what: TSMC's headquarters and its newest fabs. Most of the world's most advanced chips are made here and in Tainan. MediaTek designs phone chips here.
site.tnn.name: Tainan
site.tnn.what: TSMC's largest advanced fabs, and lines that package chips side by side with their memory.
site.tpe.name: Taipei
site.tpe.what: Headquarters of the companies that build chips into servers, laptops and racks.
site.pen.name: Penang
site.pen.what: A centre of chip assembly and test since the 1970s: chips are cut, packaged and tested here for many companies.
site.pen.who: Intel, Infineon, Micron, ASE and others
site.sgp.name: Singapore
site.sgp.what: Fabs for mature chips and memory, and lines that test and package them.
site.chn.name: Chennai
site.chn.what: Phones are now assembled here too, as phone makers spread their factories beyond China.
route.any.wafers: Silicon crystals are grown in crucibles of ultra-pure quartz, then sliced and polished into wafers, mostly in Japan, Taiwan and Germany. Chemicals and some raw materials come from many more places.
route.any.tools: The fab's machines come from a few makers. EUV scanners come only from ASML in the Netherlands, built around German mirrors and lasers. Deposition, etch and inspection tools come from the United States and Japan.
route.datacentre.design: Engineers write down what the chip must do and design it, using processor cores licensed from others and design software from a few companies. The finished design goes to the fab as files, and the masks are made from them.
route.datacentre.fab: The accelerator's dies are made in Taiwan on the most advanced lines. Each wafer goes round the loop of steps once for every layer, for months.
route.datacentre.memory: Its memory is made in stacks, mostly in Korea, and shipped to where the chip is packaged. It is often the scarcest part.
route.datacentre.package: The dies and their memory stacks are joined side by side in one package, then tested.
route.datacentre.systems: The packages are built into boards, servers and whole racks, with cooling and networking, in Taiwan, in Mexico and, more and more, in the United States.
route.datacentre.use: The racks are switched on in a data centre and run day and night for years. From the first design to the first answer, the trip takes years and crosses many countries.
route.phone.design: Phone chips are designed by phone makers and chip companies in the United States, Taiwan, China and Korea, nearly all with processor cores licensed from Arm.
route.phone.fab: Most of them are made on the most advanced lines in Taiwan, some in Korea.
route.phone.package: Each chip is packaged, often with its memory stacked on top, and tested.
route.phone.assembly: The chip goes onto a phone's board with many others, and the phone is put together, mostly in China and more and more in India and Vietnam.
route.phone.use: The phone is in your hand for a few years, charged every day.
route.car.design: Car chips come mostly from companies in Europe, Japan and the United States that design and make their own chips and sell them to the makers of car parts.
route.car.tools: Most car chips are made on older, larger processes. They need no EUV: deep-ultraviolet scanners from the Netherlands and Japan print them.
route.car.fab: They are made in the chipmakers' own fabs in Germany, Japan and elsewhere, and at foundries in Taiwan. Many of these lines are decades old and still busy.
route.car.package: They are packaged and tested, often in Malaysia, and must pass harder tests than a phone's chips: heat, cold, shaking and years of use.
route.car.modules: Makers of car parts build them into control units for the brakes, the engine, the airbags and the screens.
route.car.use: A car carries dozens of these units for many years, in heat, cold and rain.

world.design.name: Design
depth.need.name: The job
depth.need.see: A chip is built from pieces. Here is what the community is building, a small open computer, and every piece it takes: built, open, or waiting for an engine that can check it. Pick a piece: it becomes your job.
depth.logic.name: Describe
depth.logic.see: Designers describe the circuit in text, one wire per line: what each output must be, made from the inputs with AND, OR, XOR and NOT. Beside it, the table of every answer the job wants.
depth.check.name: Check
station.check.when: every pattern, before anything is built
depth.check.see: Before anything is built, the description is run against the job: every pattern of inputs goes in, and every answer is compared. A mistake found here costs minutes; found in silicon, months.
depth.gates.name: Gates
depth.gates.see: A program turns the description into gates from a library of small circuits called cells: AND, OR, XOR, inverters, flip-flops. The lit wires carry a 1 for the pattern shown.
depth.layout.name: Layout
station.layout.when: cells in rows, wires on two layers
depth.layout.see: The cells are placed in rows so their wires stay short, then joined by wires on two layers of metal, one running across and one up and down, with vias between them. Your design sits on one tile of a shared chip.
depth.masks.name: Masks
station.masks.when: one stencil per layer, to the factory
depth.masks.see: The layout is split into one stencil per layer: where the cells are, each layer of metal, the vias between. Each becomes a mask, which the factory's scanner prints onto the wafer, layer by layer.
part.need.box: your chip, still a black box
what.need.box: So far only a promise: these inputs in, these outputs out, the right answer every time.
what.need.ins: The wires coming in. Each carries a 0 or a 1; the job must be done for every mix of them.
what.need.outs: The wires going out, with the answers the job wants.
what.need.use: What the answers mean outside the chip: a sum, a lamp, a digit on a display, a count, a result inside a processor.
what.logic.code: Lines of text, one per wire: & is AND, | is OR, ^ is XOR, ~ is NOT. reg makes a wire a flip-flop, which remembers between clock ticks. Real chips are described the same way, in languages such as Verilog, only far longer.
what.logic.table: Every pattern of inputs and the answer the job wants for it. With n inputs there are 2 to the power n patterns, which is why big chips cannot be checked this way alone.
what.check.waves: Each line is a wire over time, high for 1 and low for 0, one pattern after another. Where your design's answer differs from the job's, the wire is marked in red.
what.check.verdict: One mark for each pattern: right or wrong.
what.gates.cells: Small circuits from a library, each a few transistors: the program picked and joined them to do what your text says.
what.gates.pins: Where the inputs enter the gates. A lit wire carries a 1.
what.layout.tile: Your cells in rows, and the wires between them: metal across in one colour, metal up and down in the other, small squares where they meet through a via.
what.layout.shared: Many small designs on one chip, each on its own tile, all sharing the chip's pins: a selector chooses which one is connected. Sharing makes a real chip affordable for one person. The numbered tiles are designs people have already added.
what.masks.masks: The layout split into stencils, one per layer. Real chips need dozens; the newest, about a hundred.
what.masks.reticle: A plate of quartz with the pattern in chrome, larger than the chip: the scanner shrinks its image onto the wafer.
stop.idea.need.q: Every chip starts as a job someone wrote down. Who decides what a chip should do, and what happens when the job changes after it is made?
stop.idea.need.note: A chip cannot be changed once made: a job written badly here is built into every copy.
stop.open.need.q: Could anyone design a chip? What would they need, apart from an idea?
stop.open.need.note: Open tools and shared chips have made a first design possible for one person; most of what it takes is still knowledge.
stop.divide.need.q: Should this job be a chip at all, or a program on a chip that already exists?
stop.divide.need.note: A circuit built for one job is faster and uses less energy; a program can be changed tomorrow.
stop.think.logic.q: Can a few lines of text describe a machine that will run billions of times a second?
stop.think.logic.note: Each line says what a wire must be, at every moment: the text describes a structure, not steps to follow one after another.
stop.know.logic.q: Who will read this description in ten years, when the chip is still running and its designers have moved on?
stop.know.logic.note: The text is the only full record of what the chip does: why each line is there often lives only in someone's head.
stop.fail.check.q: If every pattern you tried gave the right answer, is the design right?
stop.fail.check.note: Small circuits can be tried for every pattern; a processor has more than anyone could ever try, so checking means choosing which ones matter.
stop.idea.check.q: An AI can now write a description like this in seconds. Who checks the AI, and with what?
stop.idea.check.note: The check does not care who wrote the text: it compares the answers. The hard part is saying exactly what the job is.
stop.idea.check.tried: AI assistants that write chip descriptions from a plain request
Formal verification: proving a design right for every input, without trying them all
Checks written by one AI and reviewed by another
stop.make.gates.q: A program turns your text into gates and chooses which cells to use. What is it trying to make small: the area, the delay or the energy?
stop.make.gates.note: The same job can be built from different cells; each choice trades one of these against the others.
stop.scale.gates.q: Your design needs a handful of gates. A phone's chip has billions. How can anyone design something that large?
stop.scale.gates.note: Nobody places them one by one: designers describe blocks, reuse proven ones, and leave the gates to programs.
stop.divide.layout.q: Thousands of cells, and every wire should be short. Where should each cell go?
stop.divide.layout.note: There are more ways to place them than atoms in the universe; programs shuffle cells and keep changes that shorten the wires, like a metal cooling slowly into order.
stop.open.layout.q: One person could never pay for a chip of their own. What changes when many small designs share one?
stop.open.layout.note: Shared runs split the cost of the masks and the wafers between everyone on them; open process kits let anyone see the rules.
stop.open.layout.tried: Tiny Tapeout: hundreds of small designs on one shared chip
Open process design kits from SkyWater, GlobalFoundries and IHP
OpenROAD and OpenLane: open tools from description to layout
stop.scale.masks.q: Each newer process needs more masks, and each set costs more. Who can still afford to make a chip on the newest one?
stop.scale.masks.note: A mask set is paid once, before the first chip works: the more copies are made, the less each one carries.
stop.make.masks.q: The masks are made larger than the chip and shrunk onto it by light. Why not draw the chip directly onto each wafer?
stop.make.masks.note: Drawing with a beam is possible, but far too slow for millions of chips; a mask prints a whole chip at once.
design.proj.half.d: Adds two bits: 0 + 0, 0 + 1, 1 + 0 and 1 + 1. The first building block of every calculator and processor. Its description is already right: follow it through.
design.proj.vote.d: Spacecraft run three copies of a computer and trust the answer at least two agree on. The output is 1 when two or more inputs are 1. The description has a bug: the check will find it.
design.proj.full.d: Adds three bits: a, b and the carry from the column to the right. Chain them and you can add numbers of any size. The sum line has a bug.
design.proj.add2.d: Adds two numbers from 0 to 3 by chaining a half adder and a full adder, as processors chain them for 64-bit numbers.
design.proj.seg.d: Turns a number from 0 to 7 into the seven segments of a digital display, as in clocks and ovens. Segments a, b and c are done; d to g are left at 0.
design.proj.alu.t: ALU slice for a RISC-V core
design.proj.alu.d: One bit of a processor's arithmetic and logic unit. A RISC-V core copies it 32 times, each carry feeding the next. op1 op0 picks the job: 00 AND, 01 OR, 10 XOR, 11 ADD, and with sub = 1, ADD becomes SUBTRACT. Only AND is done.
design.proj.free.d: No job written down: four inputs, two outputs, any logic you like. The check shows what your circuit does instead of judging it.
design.proj.count.d: Counts from 0 to 7 and round again, one step per clock tick while en is 1. It must remember where it is, so it needs flip-flops: write reg in front of a line. The carry into the top bit has a bug.
design.state.errs: the description does not read: {errs} to fix
design.state.free: no job to check against: your own
design.cap.need.d: Your job is one piece of the community's computer. The box shows what the job asks for, one pattern after another; nothing is built yet.
design.cap.logic.d: Change the description in the card: each line is a wire. The table shows every answer the job wants.
design.cap.check.d: All {total} patterns run through your description; {bad} give the wrong answer. Fix the description and check again.
design.cap.gates.d: Your design became {cells} cells, about {transistors} transistors. The longest chain from an input to an output is {depth} gates.
design.cap.layout.d: Your cells placed in rows and joined by {wire} steps of wire with {vias} vias, on your own tile of a shared chip.
design.cap.masks.d: On a 130 nanometre process, a chip like yours needs about {masks} masks. Next: the factory prints them onto a wafer, at the Print station.
design.err.form: Line {l}: write each line as a name, =, and an expression.
design.err.input: Line {l}: {n} is an input. Inputs come from outside the chip and cannot be given a value.
design.err.noclock: Line {l}: this job has no clock, so it cannot use reg.
design.err.twice: Line {l}: {n} is given a value twice. In hardware each wire has exactly one source.
design.err.char: Line {l}: {n} is not understood. Use & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR) and ~ (NOT).
design.err.expr: Line {l}: the expression is incomplete or has an unmatched bracket.
design.err.undef: Line {l}: {n} is used but never given a value.
design.err.unassigned: The output {n} is never given a value.
design.err.loop: Line {l}: {n} depends on itself. Without a clock, logic must flow one way; to feed a value back, make it a flip-flop with reg.
design.wrongAt: First wrong pattern: {v}. The job wants {e}, your design gives {o}.
design.allRight: Every answer is right. Follow it on to the gates.
design.cov: At the factory's Test station, these {vectors} patterns would catch {caught}% of the faults that could happen inside your gates.
design.alu32: In a RISC-V core, this slice is copied 32 times, each carry feeding the next: 32 times {cells} cells for the core's arithmetic.
design.addYours: Add your design to the shared chip
design.addNote: Opens a form on GitHub with your design and how AI was used, filled in. The tests check it before it joins the plan; nothing is promised about a real chip yet.
design.toFab: Send the masks to the factory: {station}
design.testYours: Your design, at the Test station: {vectors} test patterns would catch {caught}% of the faults that could happen inside its gates.
build.need.computer.d: A small open computer on one shared chip, around a RISC-V core: designed piece by piece by many people, and by AI with them.
build.need.core.d: The processor: it reads instructions written in RISC-V, an open instruction set anyone may use, and does what they say.
build.need.alu.d: Adds, subtracts and compares: 32 copies of one slice, each passing its carry to the next.
build.need.slice.d: One bit of the arithmetic unit. Get it right once, and the core uses it 32 times.
build.need.adder2.d: Two adders chained: the way a carry ripples from one bit to the next.
build.need.full.d: Adds three bits; it sits inside every slice.
build.need.half.d: Adds two bits: the smallest piece of all.
build.need.regs.d: The 32 places the core keeps the numbers it works on: 1,024 register bits, and a select that says which register to write.
build.need.decode.d: Reads each instruction and sets every part of the core for it. Needs an engine that understands instructions.
build.need.timer.d: Counts clock ticks, so programs can measure time.
build.need.display.d: Shows a number on a seven-segment display.
build.need.safety.d: Runs three copies of an answer and keeps the one at least two agree on.
build.need.check.d: Catches a flipped bit with a parity check.
build.need.serial.d: Talks to the outside world one bit at a time. Needs an engine that understands timing on a wire.
build.state.engine: needs an engine to check it
build.kind.both: by a person and an AI
build.by.both: written by you and an AI
build.goal: What the community is building, and where your job fits. Pick an open piece.
build.progress: {built} of {total} pieces built · {open} open · {engine} waiting for an engine
build.proposeNeed: Propose a piece the computer needs
build.trust: Do you trust the claim, or the check? Look at the waveforms before you decide.
build.askNote: Copy this into any AI assistant. Paste its answer into the description above, and the check will judge it, line by line.
build.promptClock: This job has a clock: write reg in front of a line to make that wire a flip-flop, which keeps its value and takes the new one at each tick.
build.promptNoClock: This job has no clock: no wire may depend on itself.
build.aiUse.you: No AI: I wrote it myself.
build.aiUse.ai: An AI wrote it; I checked it in the lab.
build.aiUse.both: An AI wrote a first draft; I changed it and checked it in the lab.
build.agent.half: Done: sum is XOR, carry is AND. This is the standard half adder and covers every input.
build.agent.vote: Done: y is 1 whenever a agrees with b or with c, so any two agreeing inputs win.
build.agent.full: Done: the sum is the XOR of all three, and the carry is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.
build.agent.add2: Done: bit 0 is a half adder, bit 1 adds the carry, and s2 is the carry out of bit 1.
build.agent.seg: Done: all seven segments, simplified. g is just x2 XOR x1, which saves gates.
build.agent.alu: Done: all four operations and subtraction. The carry is the standard full-adder carry.
build.agent.count: Done: each bit flips when all the bits below it are 1, so it counts up.
build.agent.parity: Done: the XOR of all four inputs is 1 exactly when an odd number of them are 1.
build.agent.free: Here is something: y is AND, z is OR.
design.proj.parity.d: Lights when an odd number of the four inputs are 1: memories store this extra bit to catch one that flips. One input is missing from the description.
what.need.plan: Every piece the shared computer needs, joined to what needs it. Green: built and checked. Dashed: open, anyone can build it. Dotted: nothing here can check it yet; bringing an engine for it is a contribution too. The small figures say who built each piece: a person, an AI, or both.
design.proj.core.d: A processor that runs real RISC-V programs. Its arithmetic unit is your ALU slice, copied 32 times, each carry feeding the next; its registers are made of your register bit and register select once you have written them. Its decoder and memory are the lab's model for now. Its description here is a program to run on it.
core.budget.rest: decoder, program counter, control (a round estimate)
core.sliceIn: Inside: your ALU slice, {cells} cells, copied 32 times.
core.needSlice: Your ALU slice is not finished yet, so this core cannot add. Build the slice first: the core uses whatever you made.
core.ran: Your program ran: a0 = {result}, in {cycles} cycles.
core.run.loop: The program never stopped. With a wrong ALU, a loop's comparison can fail forever.
core.run.mem: Line {l}: the program reached outside the memory.
core.cap.need.d: The core is the heart of the community's computer. It is checked by real programs, so every piece inside it must be right.
core.cap.logic.d: Your program runs on the core, one instruction at a time. Every add and comparison goes through the 32 copies of your slice.
core.cap.check.d: {passed} of {tests} test programs give the right answer on your core.
core.cap.gates.d: Where the transistors go: your slice is a small part of the core, but every instruction needs it.
core.cap.layout.d: The core's floor plan: the registers, the decoder, and your slice's own layout, 32 times.
core.cap.masks.d: The masks of your slice, printed 32 times side by side in every core.
design.err.core.twice: Line {l}: the label {n} is used twice.
design.err.core.reg: Line {l}: {n} is not a register. Use x0 to x31, or names such as a0 and t1.
design.err.core.range: Line {l}: {n} is too big for this instruction. Use li for big numbers.
design.err.core.label: Line {l}: the label {n} is not defined.
design.err.core.operands: Line {l}: {n} has the wrong number of operands.
design.err.core.needM: Line {l}: {n} needs a multiplier, which this core does not have.
design.err.core.custom: Line {l}: {n} is a custom instruction this core does not have yet.
design.err.core.memop: Line {l}: write memory operands as offset(register), such as 4(a0).
design.err.core.unknown: Line {l}: {n} is not a RISC-V instruction this core knows.
fab.title: At the factory
fab.need: It will be made at a 130 nanometre factory, on a shared run with many other designs: the line in the journey is the one it will travel.
fab.logic: Every line becomes transistors the factory must print: your design needs about {transistors}.
fab.check: Passing every check makes a perfect design, not a perfect chip. The factory leaves defects: a speck, a missing via, one wire stuck. Make a copy at the factory and see what happens.
fab.checkCore: Your core passes its programs as designed. Made at the factory, one copy may have a wire stuck in one slice; then real programs go wrong.
fab.gates: How fast it runs depends on the switches the factory makes. On this process the longest path takes about {ps} picoseconds, so it could tick about {mhz} million times a second. A hotter, older or unluckier chip is slower.
fab.gatesCore: Your slice is copied 32 times: one flaw in the design, or one stuck wire from the factory, is copied into every add.
fab.layout: Your layout covers about {area} square micrometres. On the wafer, a speck that lands on a chip ruins it: the bigger the layout, the more chips a speck can ruin.
fab.masks: These {masks} masks are made once and printed onto every wafer, at the Print station. On a shared run, everyone shares their cost.
fab.defect: This copy came out with one wire stuck at {v}: {wrong} of {total} answers are now wrong, though the design is right.
fab.caught: Your {vectors} test patterns catch it: at the Test station this chip would be marked bad, not shipped. A big chip cannot be tested this completely.
fab.defectCore: This copy came out with one wire stuck in slice {bit}: only {passed} of {total} test programs still give the right answer. The design was perfect.
core.state.errs: the program does not read: {errs} to fix
api.instructions: Open Silicon Lab: a community building one open computer on a shared chip, around a RISC-V core, piece by piece, people and AI together. Read the plan (list_plan), take an open piece (get_job), write its description and check it (check_design) until it is right, see what a copy spoiled at the factory does (at_factory) and how long it lasts where it lives (life_of), then propose it (propose_design): you get a GitHub form, filled in, for a person to submit. Say honestly how AI was used. The checks are the same for everyone.
api.tool.plan: The community's plan: every piece the shared computer needs, what it is, its state (built, open, partly, or waiting for an engine that can check it) and who built it.
api.tool.job: One job: what it must do, its inputs and outputs, the rules of the description language, and the code to start from. For the core: its test programs.
api.tool.check: Check a design for a job: whether it reads, whether every answer is right (and the first wrong one), and what it becomes: gates, transistors, speed, layout, test coverage and masks. For the core: the test programs, run with the given ALU slice inside.
api.tool.factory: Make a copy of a design at the factory, with one wire left stuck: how many answers go wrong, and whether the Test station's patterns would catch it. A perfect design can still fail as a chip.
api.tool.propose: Propose a design for a piece of the plan. It is checked first; if it is right, you get the GitHub design form, filled in, for a person to submit. Nothing is posted automatically.
api.arg.job: A job (half, full, add2, vote, seg, alu, count, regbit, select, parity, free, core) or a piece of the plan (half, slice, regbit, select, timer, display, safety, check, core).
api.arg.code: The description: one wire per line, name = expression, with & | ^ ~ and brackets (reg for a flip-flop in a clocked job). For the core: a RISC-V program.
api.arg.slice: For the core: the description of the ALU slice inside it (the job alu).
api.arg.seed: Which wire the factory leaves stuck (any whole number).
api.arg.need: The piece of the plan the design is for.
api.arg.title: A short title for the design.
api.arg.author: The name or handle the design should carry.
api.arg.kind: Who wrote it: person, ai, or both.
api.arg.ai: How AI was used, in plain words: which agent, what it did, what a person changed and checked.
api.noJob: There is no job called {id}. Jobs: {jobs}.
api.noNeed: {need} is not a piece of the plan that takes a design yet.
api.kind: Say who wrote it: person, ai, or both.
api.sayAI: A design written with AI must say how AI was used.
api.notRight: The design is not right yet: fix it until every check passes, then propose it.
api.same: This exact design is already in the plan.
