debate.memory.q: AI chips do math faster than memory can feed them. Where will the next big jump in bandwidth come from?
debate.memory.v0.claim: Put memory on top of, or right beside, the compute: more HBM stacks, hybrid bonding, 3D chips.
debate.memory.v0.assumes: Heat can still escape from taller stacks, and stacked parts keep yielding well.
debate.memory.v1.claim: Spread SRAM across a wafer-sized chip so the weights never leave the silicon.
debate.memory.v1.assumes: Models fit in on-chip memory, or split across many such chips cheaply.
debate.memory.v2.claim: Smaller numbers, sparsity and computing inside memory cut the bytes that must move at all.
debate.memory.v2.assumes: Answers stay accurate enough at low precision.
debate.power.q: AI data centers ask for ever more electricity. What cuts the energy of an answer most?
debate.power.v0.claim: Each chip generation does much more work per watt; keep improving the hardware.
debate.power.v0.assumes: Process and architecture gains keep coming at the old pace.
debate.power.v1.claim: Smaller number formats and smaller models do the same job with a fraction of the work.
debate.power.v1.assumes: Quality holds as models and numbers shrink.
debate.power.v2.claim: Efficiency gains get used up by more demand; the real limit is how fast power plants and grids can grow.
debate.power.v2.assumes: Demand keeps rising whatever the chips do.
debate.shrink.q: Transistors are now stacked sheets. Where does progress come from next?
debate.shrink.v0.claim: Stacked CFET transistors and 2D-material channels keep density rising for another decade.
debate.shrink.v0.assumes: New materials and steps can be made at scale, at an affordable cost.
debate.shrink.v1.claim: Progress moves to packaging: chiplets, hybrid bonding and 3D stacks.
debate.shrink.v1.assumes: Links between dies become dense and cheap enough to behave like one chip.
debate.shrink.v2.claim: The big gains come from new kinds of computing, not from smaller switches.
debate.shrink.v2.assumes: New machines get the software and tools that today's chips have.
debate.designcost.t: The cost of designing a chip
debate.designcost.q: A leading-edge chip can cost hundreds of millions of dollars to design. How much of that can AI agents remove?
debate.designcost.v0.claim: Agents already write RTL, tests and scripts; design teams will shrink and costs fall sharply.
debate.designcost.v0.assumes: Checking an agent's work can be automated and trusted too.
debate.designcost.v1.claim: Writing was never the main cost; specification, verification and sign-off still need people, masks still cost money.
debate.designcost.v1.assumes: Judgment about what to build and what to trust stays hard to automate.
debate.open.q: Open software changed the world. Can an open instruction set, open tools and open PDKs do the same for chips?
debate.open.v0.claim: RISC-V, open tools and shared runs lower the cost of starting, so many more people can build chips.
debate.open.v0.assumes: A shared base of verified designs and tools keeps growing.
debate.open.v1.claim: Every attempt costs masks, fab time and testing; open designs do not remove the biggest costs or the need for trusted verification.
debate.supply.q: Most advanced chips pass through a few fabs and packaging lines. How should the chain be made resilient?
debate.supply.v0.claim: Build leading-edge fabs and packaging in more regions, so one shock cannot stop the world.
debate.supply.v0.assumes: Governments and customers will keep paying the higher cost.
debate.supply.v1.claim: Keep the efficient hubs and add stockpiles, second sources and long contracts.
debate.supply.v1.assumes: Shocks are short enough to ride out on buffers.
debate.signoff.q: If AI agents write most of a chip's code and tests, who is responsible when the silicon fails?
debate.signoff.v0.claim: An engineer must review and sign off; responsibility cannot be handed to a tool.
debate.signoff.v0.assumes: People can still understand and check what the agent built.
debate.signoff.v1.claim: Formal checks and coverage targets can certify an agent's work better than a tired reviewer.
debate.signoff.v1.assumes: The specification itself is complete and correct.
debate.paradigm.q: Many kinds of machine are being tried, each strong on different jobs. By 2040, will one kind win, or will computers be mixtures of many?
debate.paradigm.v0.claim: Digital chips like today's GPUs keep winning, because their software and tools are years ahead.
debate.paradigm.v0.assumes: Software and tooling matter more than raw efficiency.
debate.paradigm.v1.claim: Energy limits force mixtures: analog, optical, spiking and quantum parts each doing the job they suit.
debate.paradigm.v1.assumes: Software can split one program across very different machines.
debate.mature.q: Most chips by count come from older factories with thin margins, yet one missing part can stop a car line. Who should keep that capacity running?
debate.mature.v0.claim: After a shortage, buyers sign longer contracts and pay more for secure supply; prices do the work.
debate.mature.v0.assumes: Buyers remember shortages long enough to pay for safety.
debate.mature.v1.claim: A shortage costs far more than keeping spare capacity, so public support or shared reserves make sense.
debate.mature.v1.assumes: Support can be targeted without propping up the wrong factories.
debate.quantum.q: When will quantum computers do useful work that ordinary computers cannot?
debate.quantum.v0.claim: Reliable qubits have started to beat raw ones, and companies plan fault-tolerant machines within a few years.
debate.quantum.v0.assumes: Errors and overhead keep falling as machines grow.
debate.quantum.v1.claim: Better classical methods have challenged several advantage claims, and approximate methods already work well for many molecules.
debate.quantum.v1.assumes: Useful problems keep enough structure for classical shortcuts.
debate.bigdie.q: Bigger chips catch more defects. When does splitting a design into chiplets win?
debate.bigdie.v0.claim: Small dies yield better, can mix processes and can be reused across products.
debate.bigdie.v0.assumes: Die-to-die links are fast, cheap and low-power enough.
debate.bigdie.v1.claim: Keeping everything on one huge piece of silicon avoids slow links; spare cores route around defects.
debate.bigdie.v1.assumes: Redundancy and cooling can handle a wafer-sized chip.
debate.skills.q: When AI writes code and layouts, what will chip engineers spend their time on? Which skills last?
debate.skills.v0.claim: People set goals, review agents' work and decide trade-offs; tool-specific skills matter less.
debate.skills.v0.assumes: Agents become reliable enough to trust with whole steps.
debate.skills.v1.claim: Someone has to know why a design fails; deep knowledge of physics, timing and verification grows in value.
debate.skills.v1.assumes: Agents keep making subtle mistakes that only experts catch.

life.title: Its life
life.q: It passed every check. Will it still work in year {life}?
life.signed: It was signed off as a perfect design: a typical chip, at room temperature, on a clean supply, brand new. Out here, none of that lasts.
life.phone.story: {fleet} phones, {life} years, up to {tMax} °C. It must be cheap and fast: a phone that crashes comes back, but nobody keeps one for long.
life.car.story: {fleet} cars, {life} years, from freezing winters to {tMax} °C near the engine. A car carries hundreds of chips, so car makers count bad ones in parts per million.
life.datacentre.story: {fleet} chips running flat out, hot all day, for {life} years. In a fleet this big, an error of one in a billion per hour happens every day.
life.chart: Share of the chips shipped that have failed, year by year, by cause
life.cause.timing.d: Passed the factory's Test, then miss the clock: hot, when the supply dips under load, and as the transistors age.
life.cause.escape.d: Broken chips the test patterns did not catch. They fail almost at once.
life.cause.weak.d: Hidden flaws that pass every test, then break in the first months of use.
life.cause.wear.d: Current slowly pushes metal atoms along a wire until it breaks (electromigration).
life.req.silent: Silent wrong answers a year, across them all
life.req.cost: Cost of a good chip, against the plan
life.yield: Chips that pass the factory's Test: {v}%.
life.speed: Signed off at {mhz} MHz; sold at {sold} MHz.
life.hint.typical: Most chips fail at the factory's Test. The perfect design assumed a typical chip, and half of all chips are slower than typical. Sell it slower than it was signed off (margin).
life.hint.field: Chips pass the Test, then fail out here: hot, with the supply dipping, ageing. Testing hot at a low supply catches them at the factory instead; margin and a stronger power grid leave them room.
life.hint.escape: Broken chips slip through the Test. Your test patterns catch {cov}% of the faults they are graded on; a design whose patterns catch more lets fewer through, and testing hot catches some the patterns miss.
life.hint.weak: Weak chips pass the Test and break in their first months. Burn-in runs every chip hot for hours before it ships, so the weak ones break in the factory.
life.hint.weakBurnt: Weak chips still get through burn-in. A hot test that rejects chips unlike their neighbours screens more, and every extra copy of logic is more area where a flaw can hide.
life.hint.wear: The wires are wearing out: this chip works too hot for too long. Wider wires, a lower voltage or better cooling are what people try.
life.hint.silent: Radiation flips stored bits, and nobody notices the wrong answer. Error-correcting memory finds and fixes almost all of them.
life.hint.silentLogic: The memory is protected, but a flipped bit in the logic still gives a wrong answer nobody sees. A second copy of the logic that checks the first (lockstep) catches it, at a cost in area.
life.hint.perf: Too slow for this customer: the margin you added costs speed. A stronger power grid and a hot test can stand in for some of it.
life.hint.cost: Too expensive for this customer: every protection costs area, test time or chips thrown away. Which does this place not need?
life.hint.ok: It ships: every need here is met. Could it be cheaper or faster without breaking one? Would the same choices work in the other places?
life.margin: Margin: sold slower than signed off
life.hot: Test hot, at a low supply
life.model: A textbook model, simplified, from the earlier site: the direction and rough size of each effect matter, not the digits. Your design brings its test patterns and its slowest path.
life.notYet: Your design is not right yet. A wrong design fails everywhere; this is the life it would have once it is right.
life.teaser: Passing every check means it is right at the conditions it was checked at. Then it is made, tested and shipped, and lives for years somewhere hot, shaken and far from typical.
api.tool.life: Its life: a design, made and shipped to a phone, a car or a data centre, lived year by year. Which causes fail it (too slow out there, defects the test missed, weak spots, wires wearing out), radiation's silent wrong answers, and whether that place's needs are met, for the choices made in the design and at the factory. Why a perfect design still fails.

way.title: Another way to compute
way.note: A judgment, not a measurement: where things stand changes fast.
way.add: Add a way, or correct this one
way.saves.energy: the energy each step of computing costs
way.saves.data: the cost of moving data, not computing with it
way.super.how: In metals cooled close to absolute zero, current flows with no resistance at all. Logic built from them switches with tiny pulses of magnetic flux, and wastes almost nothing.
way.super.catch: Everything must be kept colder than outer space, the circuits are far less dense than today's, and the cooling costs energy of its own.
way.super.now: Teams are designing such chips for AI data centres, betting the savings outweigh the cooling.
way.photonic.how: Light carries data between chips without heating the wires, and beams that interfere can do a whole matrix of multiply-adds as they pass.
way.photonic.catch: Turning electrical numbers into light and back costs energy and precision, and light is hard to store.
way.photonic.now: Light already carries data between racks and is moving onto the package; light that computes is still early.
way.spatial.how: Instead of fetching numbers from memory chips, the whole program is laid out across a very large chip, each tile keeping its numbers beside it, and data flows from tile to tile.
way.spatial.catch: A model must fit in the chip's own memory, and a chip the size of a wafer needs its own answers to defects, power and heat.
way.spatial.now: Sold today for AI, where its makers lead on speed for each user.
way.approx.how: Use fewer bits where nobody notices the small errors: AI models run well on numbers of 8, 4 or even fewer bits, and a smaller number is cheaper to move and multiply.
way.approx.catch: It only works where errors are tolerable, and someone must check that they are.
way.neuro.how: Like neurons, its parts send a spike only when something changes, and spend almost nothing while nothing happens.
way.neuro.catch: Most software is not written for spikes, and training spiking networks is still hard.
way.neuro.now: Research chips and small products that listen or watch all the time on a tiny battery.
way.analog.how: Voltages stand for numbers, and a circuit solves an equation continuously instead of step by step.
way.analog.catch: Noise limits precision, and each problem needs the circuit rewired.
way.analog.now: Small companies sell analog computers again, for control and for solving equations.
way.cim.how: Do the multiply-adds inside the memory cells, where the numbers are stored, so they never travel over the busy wires.
way.cim.catch: Analog cells drift and differ from one another, and big models outgrow the arrays.
way.cim.now: Prototype and early product chips, mostly for small AI models.
way.reversible.how: Logic that throws no information away does not have to pay the floor for erasing it, and the energy of a switch can be recycled instead of turned into heat.
way.reversible.catch: It is slower, needs more transistors, and a whole computer built this way has never been made.
way.reversible.now: Test chips, and a few companies starting to build them.
way.pbits.how: Bits that flicker between 0 and 1 on purpose, made from switches too small to sit still. Wired together, they settle into good answers to search and sampling problems.
way.pbits.catch: Only some problems fit, and making the noise behave is an engineering problem of its own.
way.quantum.how: Qubits hold many possibilities at once, and interference steers them toward answers some problems need, such as simulating molecules.
way.quantum.catch: Qubits lose their state at the slightest disturbance; useful machines need error correction, with many physical qubits for every reliable one.
way.quantum.now: Prototype machines; error-corrected ones are the race now.
floor.title: The floor
floor.q: How far is your chip from what physics allows?
floor.energy: Erasing one bit of information costs at least kT ln 2 (Landauer's limit): about {zj} zeptojoules at room temperature. Ordinary logic erases bits all the time, so this is the floor under every step.
floor.yours: Your chip spends about {times} times the floor on each multiply-add: its arithmetic alone is {math} times, and {moving}% of the energy goes to fetching numbers. Physics leaves a lot of room. What stands in the way is engineering.
floor.room: At room temperature, the floor is as above. A colder chip has a lower one: try it.
floor.cold: At {k} K, the chip's floor is {pct}% of the room's. But its heat must be pumped out to the room, and even a perfect refrigerator spends {pump}% of the total doing it: exactly the room's floor again. Real refrigerators do worse. Cooling cannot lower the floor; it can make real switches waste less, which is the bet of superconducting logic.
floor.speed: At your clock ({ghz} billion ticks a second in this model), light in glass travels about {cm} cm in one tick. Your chip is {mm} mm corner to corner: at least {ticks} of a tick to cross. Real wires are many times slower than light, so the slowest signal must cross far less.

game.oneChip: You have one chip: its settings carry from challenge to challenge, so a change for one goal can undo another.
game.own.half: Adds two bits: 0 + 0, 0 + 1, 1 + 0 and 1 + 1, giving a sum and a carry. The first building block of every calculator and processor. This description has one bug: check it, and the table shows which row goes wrong.
game.job.goal: Design this piece of the shared computer: {job}. When the check passes, add it to the plan.
game.spot.d: The factory made four copies of the full adder, and one is broken. Run up to {tests} test patterns on all four, then say which copy is broken.
game.spot.fine: Copy {chip} is fine. Look for the column that differs from what it should be.
game.spot.missed: None of your patterns caught it: the broken copy gets these right. Real testers face this too: which few patterns catch the most faults?
game.spot.found: Yes: copy {chip} is broken, and your patterns caught it.
game.ch.half.goal: Fix the half adder so it adds two bits right.
game.ch.half.why: Every chip starts as a description of what it should do. A computer turns it into gates and wires, so a mistake here is copied into every chip made.
game.ch.vote.goal: Fix the majority voter that spacecraft trust.
game.ch.vote.why: An AI will offer a fix here, and sound sure about it. The check decides, not the confidence.
game.ch.full.goal: Fix the sum line of the full adder.
game.ch.full.why: Chain full adders and you can add numbers of any size. One wrong row, and every sum that passes through it can be wrong.
game.ch.months.why: A wafer goes round the factory's machines dozens of times, one layer per lap. A factory running full earns the most, and makes every wafer wait.
game.ch.quick.t: A chip that is quick to make
game.ch.quick.why: Some chips are needed fast: a first test chip, a part for a car line that has stopped. Fewer layers mean fewer laps.
game.ch.spot.goal: Run a few test patterns and find the copy the factory broke.
game.ch.spot.why: One speck of dust can break a wire. Nobody can try every input on every chip, so testers choose the patterns that catch the most faults.
game.ch.cores.why: A wafer holds a fixed area. A bigger chip holds more cores, but one flaw throws more of it away.
game.ch.phone.goal: Choose what the design and the factory do, so a phone's chip lives through its years.
game.ch.phone.why: A phone is cheap, warm in a pocket and replaced after a few years. What it needs is not what a car needs.
game.ch.car.goal: Make a car's chip last for years in heat and cold, with failures counted in parts per million.
game.ch.car.why: A car carries hundreds of chips, and one that fails can stop it on the road. Car makers ask for almost none to fail.
game.ch.dclife.goal: Keep a data centre's chips right while they run flat out and hot, with no silent errors.
game.ch.dclife.why: In a fleet this big, a one-in-a-billion fault happens every day, and a wrong answer nobody notices is worse than a crash.
game.ch.fed.why: A chip computes fast, then waits for numbers to arrive from memory. Moving data costs more time and energy than computing with it.
game.ch.fast.why: For decades chips got faster every year. Now the slowest signal and the heat set the limit.
